summary: This is the first part of the Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) specification. It defines how to encrypt email messages and authenticate their senders for transfer over Internet mail. It is historic.

eli5.summary: This paper explains how to put your email in a locked box and sign it so only the right person can read it and they know it came from you. It is historic.

questions: what is a mic in pem
subtitle: How Privacy Enhanced Mail encrypts, signs and encodes an email message from sender to recipient.

tldr.problem: Internet mail travels in the clear through relays, so messages can be read or altered and a sender cannot be sure who wrote one. Any fix also has to survive SMTP and the different text conventions of mail systems.
tldr.mechanism: Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) works end to end at or above the user agent. The sender puts the text into a canonical form, computes a message integrity check (MIC), optionally encrypts it, encodes it in a 64-character printable alphabet, and wraps it with header fields that carry the keys and parameters.
tldr.outcome: PEM offers disclosure protection, originator authenticity, message integrity and, with asymmetric keys, non-repudiation of origin. RFC 1421 is Historic.

facts.label: Printable encoding
facts.value: 6 bits per character, 4 characters per 24 bits

today: RFC 1421 is Historic. It obsoletes RFC 1113, and the metadata records no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It was written to work with RFC 1422, RFC 1423 and RFC 1424.

sections.title: Goals and Services
sections.content:
RFC 1421 defines message encryption and authentication procedures for Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) on the Internet. It is the first of a set of four RFCs: RFC 1422 covers key management with public-key certificates, RFC 1423 covers algorithms and identifiers, and RFC 1424 covers formats and procedures for the key management infrastructure.

The services are confidentiality, authentication, message integrity and, when asymmetric key management is used, non-repudiation of origin. They are applied end to end between sender and recipient at or above the User Agent level, so the Message Transfer System and relay sites need no changes. Security services apply to the whole message body, not to parts of it. Authentication, integrity and non-repudiation are always applied, while confidentiality is optional.

The RFC lists what it does not address, including access control, traffic flow confidentiality, routing control, proof of receipt and replay prevention. Its scope is RFC 822 text mail, signalled by the Content-Domain value RFC822.
sections.eli5: PEM is a sealed, signed envelope that you prepare at home. The post office just carries it and does not need any new rules.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Keys
sections.content:
PEM uses a two-level keying hierarchy. A Data Encrypting Key (DEK) encrypts the message text and, with some algorithms, helps compute the MIC. DEKs are generated for each message, so nothing needs to be shared in advance. An Interchange Key (IK) encrypts the DEK for transmission, with one version of the DEK per named recipient. The same IK is usually used for all messages from one sender to one recipient over a period of time.

With symmetric key management, the IK is a single secret shared by sender and recipient, and it encrypts both the DEK and the MIC. With asymmetric key management, the recipient's public component encrypts the DEK, and the sender's private component signs the MIC, so only one signed MIC is needed no matter how many recipients there are. The RFC calls these the public and private components to avoid confusion with other uses of the word key.

Each IK comes from an Issuing Authority, which is a Certification Authority in the certificate-based scheme of RFC 1422. The RFC recommends generating DEKs on a one-time, per-message basis. It does not say how IKs are distributed.
sections.eli5: For each letter you make a brand-new key to lock it. Then you put that key in a small box that only your friend's own key can open and send both together.

sections.title: Turning a Message into a PEM Message
sections.content:
Mail systems disagree about character sets and line endings, and SMTP needs 7-bit ASCII, lines of at most 1000 characters, and no stray end-of-message sequence. Raw ciphertext would be broken by these conversions. So PEM applies four steps, with the combined form Encode(Encrypt(Canonicalize(Local_Form))).

  • Local form: the text in the host's native character set and line convention.
  • Canonical form: ASCII text with CR LF line delimiters, like the inter-SMTP form but without dot-stuffing. How to get there depends on the local system and is not specified.
  • Authentication and encryption: the MIC is computed over the canonical form with no padding added. Encryption, for ENCRYPTED messages only, uses the padding technique of RFC 1423.
  • Printable encoding: each 24-bit group becomes 4 characters from a 64-character subset, 6 bits per character, with = as padding. Output lines are exactly 64 characters, except the last.

The receiver reverses these steps in order and validates the MIC before converting to its own local form.
sections.eli5: First you copy your note in neat standard handwriting, then you lock it up, then you rewrite the locked note using only letters and digits so nothing gets scrambled in the post.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Header Fields
sections.content:
PEM messages are encapsulated using the technique of RFC 934, so to the mail system the whole message is just body text. The message starts with the boundary line -----BEGIN PRIVACY-ENHANCED MESSAGE-----, followed by an encapsulated header, a blank line, the encapsulated text, and the boundary -----END PRIVACY-ENHANCED MESSAGE-----. PEM messages can be nested, and ordinary text can sit between them.

The header fields carry the cryptographic control information. Proc-Type is required and first, with version 4 and a message type. Content-Domain comes second. DEK-Info names the text encryption algorithm and any parameters such as an IV. Originator-ID and Originator-Certificate identify the sender's key, and Issuer-Certificate carries the certificates above it. MIC-Info carries the signed MIC for asymmetric recipients. Each recipient gets a Recipient-ID field and a Key-Info field holding the DEK encrypted under that recipient's IK. Algorithm identifiers are defined in RFC 1423.

Field names no longer begin with the old X- prefix. Implementations should accept the prefix on incoming fields but not emit it.
sections.eli5: The locked letter comes with a cover note listing what kind of lock was used and a small key box for each person who may open it.

sections.title: Message Types and Mailing Lists
sections.content:
There are four Proc-Type values. ENCRYPTED applies all services, including confidentiality. MIC-ONLY applies all but confidentiality, and still uses the printable encoding to protect the text from changes in transit. MIC-CLEAR is signed but not encoded, so people without PEM software can still read it, but its MIC may fail for harmless reasons if the mail system changes the text. A failed MIC on a MIC-CLEAR message therefore does not necessarily mean an attack. CRL carries Certificate Revocation Lists and no text.

An ENCRYPTED message should not be forwarded as is, because the new recipients lack the DEK. The forwarder must first reduce it to MIC-ONLY or MIC-CLEAR, keeping the original MIC.

For mailing lists, the sender can encrypt the DEK separately for each member (IK-per-recipient) or use one key for the list name (IK-per-list). The RFC points out that a shared list key is widely exposed, is hard to revoke, and lets any holder masquerade as another originator. For asymmetric keys it recommends a PEM-capable list exploder that reduces incoming ENCRYPTED messages and re-encrypts them for each member.
sections.eli5: You can send a sealed secret letter, or a signed letter anyone can read, or a signed letter that is rewritten so the mail cannot smudge it. For a club, it is safer to lock a copy separately for each member.

sections.title: Minimum Requirements
sections.content:
A complete PEM implementation must support at least one of the symmetric and asymmetric key management modes. Support for the certificate-based procedures of RFC 1422 is strongly encouraged, and such implementations must display user names in X.500 distinguished name form. A full implementation should send and receive ENCRYPTED, MIC-ONLY and MIC-CLEAR messages, receive CRL messages, support nested and annotated messages, and be able to reduce ENCRYPTED messages for forwarding.

The RFC also gives the full grammar of a PEM message in RFC 822 notation. Its text includes example messages for the symmetric and asymmetric cases.
sections.eli5: A real PEM program has to handle every kind of letter and be able to repackage a secret one so it can be passed along.

viz.caption: PEM MESSAGE TYPES (RFC 1421, PROC-TYPE SECOND SUBFIELD)

items.label: Full protection
items.desc: Confidentiality, authentication, integrity and, with asymmetric keys, non-repudiation of origin.

items.label: Signed and encoded
items.desc: All services except confidentiality; text is printably encoded.

items.label: Signed, readable
items.desc: Same services as MIC-ONLY, but no printable encoding, so it is readable without PEM software.

items.label: Revocation lists
items.desc: Transfers Certificate Revocation Lists; no user text.

data.title: Encapsulated message layout
data.code:
-----BEGIN PRIVACY-ENHANCED MESSAGE-----
<encapsulated header: Proc-Type, Content-Domain, DEK-Info, ...>

<encapsulated text, 64 printable characters per line>
-----END PRIVACY-ENHANCED MESSAGE-----
